The metabolic biomachine: from chemical processing to flux exponent control

Specify the function and the constraints of the machine. Use optimization to select behavior. Retain the biochemical structure needed for the question.

CCBS · Lecture 13 · core · 22 October 2026 · 10:40–12:15

A cellular decision has to become physical work. Lecture 12 asked how molecular interactions select an action. The cell must now supply that action with material and energy. Metabolism is the chemical-processing function that makes this possible.

We will follow one ATP-producing machine through three levels of knowledge. First, a known enzyme law predicts how glycolysis responds to ATP demand. Next, we describe behavior through an objective and biochemical constraints, then simplify that problem to ask what flux balance analysis can establish. Finally, we restore the structure of binding and catalysis through flux exponent control. Each change answers a question the previous model leaves open.1

Ten teaching points in three parts. The figures and experiments work offline. Present, or the P key, shows the graphical route. The optional calculations retain supporting derivations.

Companion reading and classroom demonstrations

Use the five classroom demonstrations alongside Parts 2 and 3. The exposition works through the derivations and solved checkpoints. The lineage explains the questions behind these modeling methods. The research essay asks which constraints determine each prediction. The worked extension tests whether maximum growth identifies a pathway.

Part 1 · Begin with a metabolic machine whose kinetics we know

Compare the available control actions. Then follow ATP production through a change in demand.

1Different components give chemical-processing machines different control actions

The biomachine perspective starts with a function. How do cells and human-engineered machines achieve chemical processing, and which principles survive the change of components?

The accounting and control questions are shared. Both machines must obtain feedstock, convert it into useful products and respond to changing demand. Material conservation applies to each. Feedback must correct disturbances through physically available actuators. Lecture 10 used this comparison for adaptation. Here the controlled process is metabolism.

A chemical plant can organize reactions across different physical environments. Separate vessels can have different temperatures, pressures and residence times. Pumps and valves regulate feeding, transfer and withdrawal. A laboratory chemist can also change the conditions in a test tube. Much of chemical-process control concerns these environments and flows.

A cell achieves selectivity mainly through molecules within compatible operating conditions. Raising the temperature to accelerate one desired reaction would also affect many other reactions and the proteins that carry them out. Instead, enzymes accelerate selected conversions. Binding changes which enzyme states are occupied and active. Synthesis and removal change how much enzyme is available.

Cells also regulate transport, pH and compartmentalization through molecular machinery. These actions must remain compatible with cell function. To define our model, fix the cell type, condition and time window. Take the available catalytic conversions as given and ask how their enzyme activities can vary.

P1The same chemical-processing task must be controlled through different physical components.

Binding and catalysis give this comparison a mathematical starting point. Lecture 8 separated fast redistribution among bound states from catalytic changes to molecular totals. At that resolution, the catalytic reaction list determines how the totals can change. Enzyme regulation determines how fast those changes happen. The cell can thus coordinate many conversions in a shared chemical environment without giving every reaction its own heated vessel.

Identify the chemical-processing function, the available actuators and the conditions held fixed before choosing a metabolic model.

2ATP production must first invest ATP

Glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate through a sequence of enzyme-catalyzed reactions. To expose its control problem, follow the ATP bookkeeping through that sequence: ATP must be spent before more ATP is made.

The full pathway has an investment phase and a payoff phase. Hexokinase and phosphofructokinase each consume one ATP per glucose. Cleavage produces two three-carbon intermediates. Each passes through phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase, so those two steps together return four ATP per glucose. The net yield is two ATP.

One conversion junction can collect several reactants and products. In the diagrams, a shared double chevron marks an overall conversion. All branches entering that junction are consumed by the same conversion. All branches leaving it are produced. A path from ATP to intermediate therefore does not imply that ATP is its only substrate. Glucose supplies the chemical free energy and carbon.

Retain the ATP pool and a lumped intermediate pool. Count pathway throughput per three-carbon intermediate equivalent, so each effective investment event receives half a glucose, consumes one ATP and makes one intermediate unit. The payoff event consumes that intermediate unit and returns two ATP. This changes the throughput convention, not the ATP concentration unit.

Let qIq_I be the lumped intermediate concentration and qATPq_{\mathrm{ATP}} the ATP concentration. As in Lecture 8, qq denotes a modeled total after fast binding has been eliminated. The investment and payoff fluxes are v1v_1 and v2v_2. The external demand ww consumes ATP to do work. Glucose remains an available external feed.

The same argument applies to any positive ATP investment. An investment of ν\nu ATP units followed by a payoff of ν+1\nu+1 has the same net yield. All simulations below use ν=1\nu=1.

P2Making more ATP requires spending ATP before the payoff arrives.

Each reaction contributes one column to the concentration balance. A positive stoichiometric entry produces a pool and a negative entry consumes it. With q=(qI,qATP)Tq=(q_I,q_{\mathrm{ATP}})^{\mathsf T} and v=(v1,v2)Tv=(v_1,v_2)^{\mathsf T},

dqdt=Sv+Sww.\boxed{\frac{dq}{dt}=S v+S^w w.}
S=(1−1−12),Sw=(0−1).S=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad S^w=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
dqIdt=v1−v2,dqATPdt=−v1+2v2−w.\frac{dq_I}{dt}=v_1-v_2,\qquad\frac{dq_{\mathrm{ATP}}}{dt}=-v_1+2v_2-w.

Fluxes have units of concentration per time. The one-invested, two-returned convention corresponds to two invested and four returned per glucose. The reduced model retains only intermediate and ATP accumulation. Feed, ADP, phosphate, redox partners and carbon products remain outside those retained pools. Each conversion is a composite process.3

The matrix specifies the consequences of a reaction, not its kinetic rate. Genome annotation and biochemical curation help identify possible catalytic conversions. They do not usually supply every binding affinity, allosteric interaction, enzyme amount or effective rate law. Here we begin with a well-studied example for which a useful effective regulatory law is available.

Read the investment, payoff and external demand directly into dq/dt=Sv+Swwdq/dt=S v+S^w w. Keep stoichiometry separate from enzyme kinetics.

3ATP feedback can regulate demand and produce oscillation

To predict a trajectory, we now supply the missing rate laws. The example will show both why negative feedback helps and why stronger regulation can create a dynamical problem.

The regulatory rate laws are hard-won biochemical knowledge. A reaction inventory tells us which molecules are consumed and produced. It does not tell us how enzyme activity changes with ATP. Researchers purified glycolytic enzymes, measured activity across substrate and effector concentrations, and later tested candidate binding sites by mutation. Those experiments established ATP's dual role as substrate and regulator of phosphofructokinase.1011

Genome-based reaction annotation can scale across many enzymes, followed by curation of the reconstruction. Establishing regulatory kinetics still requires enzyme-specific experiments. Each activity curve depends on the substrates, effectors and assay conditions held fixed.

The payoff feedback also has a biochemical basis. Macfarlane and Ainsworth measured inhibition of purified yeast pyruvate kinase by its product MgATP while controlling free magnesium. This supports retaining a negative ATP dependence in the effective payoff step. It does not establish the particular Hill denominator below. 12

The two Hill laws below compress that knowledge into an illustrative model. They represent ATP investment and effective feedback, rather than a fit of one organism's complete glycolytic kinetics. The chosen exponents and rate scale are teaching parameters.

Choose a common concentration scale and a metabolic clock. Write qˉI=qI/q0\bar q_I=q_I/q_0, qˉATP=qATP/q0\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}=q_{\mathrm{ATP}}/q_0, tˉ=t/tmet\bar t=t/t_{\mathrm{met}}, vˉ=v/(q0/tmet)\bar v=v/(q_0/t_{\mathrm{met}}) and wˉ=w/(q0/tmet)\bar w=w/(q_0/t_{\mathrm{met}}). The same stoichiometric equations hold for barred quantities, with derivatives taken with respect to tˉ\bar t. These simulations illustrate behavior rather than fitting a measured clock.

High ATP inhibits the enzymes that supply it. The effective laws used in the flux exponent control paper are

vˉ1=2qˉATP1+qˉATP2h,vˉ2=2κqˉI1+qˉATP2g,κ=1.1,g=0.3.\bar v_1=\frac{2\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}}{1+\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}^{2h}},\qquad \bar v_2=\frac{2\kappa\bar q_I}{1+\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}^{2g}},\qquad \kappa=1.1,\quad g=0.3.

The numerator of the first rate retains the need to invest ATP. The denominator represents inhibition by ATP. The second rate retains dependence on the intermediate and a weaker ATP inhibition. The adjustable parameter hh changes the strength of upstream inhibition. These Hill-type functions are effective kinetic laws, not a reconstruction of every binding step.1

At baseline demand, the same operating point exists for every feedback strength. For wˉ=1\bar w=1, the pools (qˉI∗,qˉATP∗)=(1/κ,1)(\bar q_I^*,\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}^*)=(1/\kappa,1) give vˉ1∗=vˉ2∗=1\bar v_1^*=\bar v_2^*=1. After demand rises, a drop in ATP relieves inhibition and increases supply. Whether the pools settle depends on the strength and timing of this feedback.

The demand step first creates a supply deficit. Immediately before the step, both pathway fluxes equal one. Demand rises to 1.1 while the concentrations, and hence the kinetic rates, are still unchanged. At that instant,

dqˉIdtˉ∣0+=0,dqˉATPdtˉ∣0+=1−1.1=−0.1.\left.\frac{d\bar q_I}{d\bar t}\right|_{0^+}=0,\qquad\left.\frac{d\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}}{d\bar t}\right|_{0^+}=1-1.1=-0.1.

ATP therefore falls before supply catches up. Lower ATP relieves inhibition. The ensuing flux changes alter both pools, which change the rates again. This feedback loop can settle or continue oscillating, as the three trajectories show.

P3The same pathway can return toward its operating level, ring, or oscillate under different regulation.

Steady compensation improves as upstream inhibition strengthens. At a nearby balanced state, vˉ1=wˉ\bar v_1=\bar w. Differentiating the first rate at baseline gives

(1−h) δqˉATP∗=δwˉ,∂qˉATP∗∂wˉ=11−h.(1-h)\,\delta\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}^*=\delta\bar w,\qquad\frac{\partial\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}^*}{\partial\bar w}=\frac{1}{1-h}.

For h>1h>1, a demand increase leaves a negative ATP offset. Increasing hh reduces its local magnitude. This is homeostatic compensation with a finite error. It is not the robust perfect adaptation established by an integral-memory construction in Lecture 10.

The improvement has a stability limit in this architecture. The local stability calculation in A2 shows that baseline perturbations decay in the linearized dynamics precisely when

1<h<1+κ+2g=2.7.\boxed{1<h<1+\kappa+2g=2.7.}

The feedback that reduces the steady error eventually destabilizes this operating point. ATP investment helps explain the difficulty: increasing upstream throughput spends ATP immediately, before the downstream payoff. The optional calculation connects this architecture to the control limitations discussed in Lecture 10. The result does not make oscillation inevitable for every controller or every cell.

Conservation of robustness connects this steady improvement to sensitivity at other frequencies. Lecture 10, appendix A20, introduced the Bode sensitivity integral during the discussion of adaptation. A slowly varying disturbance tests steady regulation. What exact ATP restoration costs in this architecture

The present scalar feedback cannot remove the ATP offset while remaining stable. Within 1<h<2.71<h<2.7, the magnitude of the steady demand sensitivity is 1/(h−1)>1/1.71/(h-1)>1/1.7. Increasing hh alone reaches instability before this error can vanish. This supports a reason to tolerate a finite offset within this regulatory architecture.

Adding a memory changes the architecture and the conclusion. To test the implication, let x=δqˉIx=\delta\bar q_I, y=δqˉATPy=\delta\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}} and d=δwˉd=\delta\bar w. Let α=δlog⁡u1\alpha=\delta\log u_1 be a small change in upstream log activity, so δvˉ1=y+α\delta\bar v_1=y+\alpha. Retain δvˉ2=κx−gy\delta\bar v_2=\kappa x-gy. Introduce an error memory η\eta and a positive integral gain kIk_I:

α=−hy+kIη,η′=−y.\alpha=-hy+k_I\eta,\qquad\eta'=-y.

Low ATP now both relieves the instantaneous inhibition and accumulates a persistent activity adjustment. This is a hypothetical controller used to test the mathematical claim. It is not an identification of a glycolytic molecular memory.

Every equilibrium of this controller restores ATP, provided the equilibrium is reached. The memory equation requires y∗=0y^*=0. For constant demand displacement dd, the balances then give x∗=d/κx^*=d/\kappa and η∗=d/kI\eta^*=d/k_I. Stability is an additional requirement.

χ(s)=s3+(2.7−h)s2+[1.1(h−1)−kI]s+1.1kI.\chi(s)=s^3+(2.7-h)s^2+\left[1.1(h-1)-k_I\right]s+1.1k_I.

A restricted range of integral gains gives stable exact adaptation. The cubic Routh–Hurwitz conditions reduce to

1<h<2.7,0<kI<1.1(h−1)(2.7−h)3.8−h.\boxed{1<h<2.7,\qquad 0<k_I<\frac{1.1(h-1)(2.7-h)}{3.8-h}.}

Both feedback gains determine stability. Near h=2.7h=2.7, the allowed positive integral gain shrinks to zero. At h=2h=2, a nonzero range remains. Pure integral feedback with h=0h=0 cannot stabilize this plant. Integral action can therefore add precision or cause instability, depending on the surrounding regulation.

Instability is not restricted to a large demand change. The local poles do not depend on the size of dd. Halving a small step halves its response but does not change stability or decay rate. A nonlinear response to a large disturbance requires a separate calculation.

The control tradeoff suggests a biological hypothesis rather than settling the biological question. Precise ATP restoration may compete with transient regulation, enzyme cost and other tasks. The stable integral-memory cases still obey the same weighted sensitivity identity. Eliminating zero-frequency error still requires amplification at other frequencies. It does not establish that perfect adaptation is unimportant in metabolism, or that a stable memory mechanism cannot achieve it. This is the same distinction between an adapting equilibrium and a stable route to that equilibrium developed in Lecture 10.

Then θ=y\theta=y for matching initial values of position and velocity. The animation uses x(0)=0x(0)=0, y(0)=0.04y(0)=0.04, θ(0)=0.04\theta(0)=0.04 and θ′(0)=(h−1−2g)0.04\theta'(0)=(h-1-2g)0.04.
