This correspondence concerns the local dynamics, not every input-output property. At h=g=0h=g=0, an independently applied pivot torque drives pendulum angle through 1/[s2+(κ+1)s−κ]1/[s^2+(\kappa+1)s-\kappa], which has no finite zero. A small change in upstream log activity drives ATP through (κ−s)/[s2+(κ+1)s−κ](\kappa-s)/[s^2+(\kappa+1)s-\kappa], which has a right-half-plane zero at s=κs=\kappa. That additional limitation expresses the immediate ATP cost of upstream investment. The positive eigenvalue and the right-half-plane zero are different facts. The motor feedback above reproduces the local metabolic equation, not all possible metabolic actuators.

Use an explicit rate law to distinguish a balanced state, a stable return, a finite steady error and an oscillation. Negative feedback alone does not guarantee a stable or precise response.

We have predicted a pathway's response by specifying its enzyme laws. Can we instead describe the function the machine should achieve and the biochemical restrictions it must obey?

Part 2 · Specify metabolic function through objectives and constraints

First formulate the behavior as an optimization problem. Then relax constraints, solve a steady task explicitly and scale up to a curated organism.

4Describe behavior through an objective and biochemical constraints

A complex behavior can be easier to specify by its purpose and physical restrictions than by writing every regulatory response that produces it. Constraint-based modeling starts from this alternative way of describing a machine.

A specified regulatory law determines how the machine responds at each state. In Part 1, the Hill functions gave the reaction fluxes from the current concentrations. Denote such a fully specified flux law by vlaw(q)v_{\mathrm{law}}(q). With an imposed demand w(t)w(t), we predict a trajectory by integrating

q˙(t)=Svlaw(q(t))+Sww(t),q(0)=qinit.\dot q(t)=S v_{\mathrm{law}}(q(t))+S^w w(t),\qquad q(0)=q^{\mathrm{init}}.

The vector qq contains the retained concentrations. The matrices SS and SwS^w convert reaction fluxes and external demand into concentration changes. A controller with memory would add its internal states. For a large machine, specifying all these responses can be the difficult part.

An optimization describes the behavior by what it achieves and what it must obey. Fix the same initial state, demand history and time interval [0,T][0,T]. Let Cbio\mathcal C_{\mathrm{bio}} contain the concentration and flux histories permitted by the biochemical model. Let J[q,v]\mathcal J[q,v] measure the function to be achieved, such as useful production with a cost for ATP depletion. When the optimum is attained, select

(q∗(⋅),v∗(⋅))∈arg max⁡(q(⋅),v(⋅))∈Cbio J[q,v].\boxed{(q^*(\cdot),v^*(\cdot))\in\underset{(q(\cdot),v(\cdot))\in\mathcal C_{\mathrm{bio}}}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}\ \mathcal J[q,v].}

The biochemical constraints describe the machinery available to achieve that function. They include the balance q˙=Sv+Sww\dot q=Sv+S^w w, initial state, nonnegative pools and the substrate, catalytic, binding, resource and actuator restrictions of the declared model. The histories must be compatible with any required enzyme or controller states. Regulation remains a choice within its physical and information restrictions. At this stage, we have not removed any restriction from that model.

P4Describe a machine's behavior by optimizing its function subject to the constraints of its components.

This is a central use of the biomachine perspective. We often understand a crane, car or computer through its overall task, the responsibilities of its modules and the limits at their interfaces. Those specifications can be compact even when the resulting behavior is complicated. An objective and constraints provide such a description for metabolism. Finding their solution can still require substantial computation.

The objective is a biological or design hypothesis. For a designed controller, it states what we want the machine to do. For a cell, it states a proposed function whose predictions must be compared with measurements. An optimum need not be unique, and an observed cell need not attain it. A complete biochemical constraint set means complete within the declared model boundary, not a description of every process in the cell.

The optional extension below develops this perspective through machine hierarchy, a solved static-to-dynamic-to-control example, variational mechanics and learning. The spoken route now asks how to make a biochemical optimization easier to solve.

Relax constraints to obtain easier problems and performance bounds

Relaxation is an operation on an already specified optimization problem. Keep the task, initial conditions, demand, horizon and objective fixed. Removing restrictions enlarges the set of permitted histories. Write two such enlargements as C1\mathcal C_1 and C2\mathcal C_2. If the actual history belongs to Cbio\mathcal C_{\mathrm{bio}}, then

Cbio⊆C1⊆C2⟹Jactual≤Jbio∗≤J1∗≤J2∗.\mathcal C_{\mathrm{bio}}\subseteq\mathcal C_1\subseteq\mathcal C_2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal J_{\mathrm{actual}}\leq\mathcal J^*_{\mathrm{bio}}\leq\mathcal J^*_1\leq\mathcal J^*_2.

Each star denotes the supremum of the same score over the indicated set. The supremum is a maximum when attained. A larger set can give a looser upper bound, but its simpler constraints can make that bound computable. For a minimized cost, enlarging the set instead gives a lower bound.15

A useful bound can precede a detailed mechanism. The Carnot bound η≤1−Tcold/Thot\eta\leq1-T_{\mathrm{cold}}/T_{\mathrm{hot}} limits heat-engine efficiency using absolute reservoir temperatures. Metabolic conservation and resource constraints can similarly limit performance before the detailed regulation is known. The mechanism matters for whether the machine can approach that bound.

Near-optimal performance makes an optimizer a candidate explanation. If selection favors the stated function under the retained constraints, flux allocations near the optimum become hypotheses for cellular behavior. Agreement with measurements supports that joint choice of objective and constraints. A gap can reflect omitted restrictions or another task the cell must perform.

The most direct relaxation treats every reaction flux as an adjustable trajectory. Over a duration TT, we could maximize a performance functional J[q,v]\mathcal J[q,v] subject to

dqdt=Sv+Sww,q(0)=qinit,q(t)≥0,ℓ≤v(t)≤u.\frac{dq}{dt}=S v+S^w w,\qquad q(0)=q^{\mathrm{init}},\qquad q(t)\geq0,\qquad\ell\leq v(t)\leq u.

Here ℓ\ell and uu are lower and upper flux bounds. This is an optimal-control problem. To see how much control the relaxation grants, first consider freely adjustable fluxes before imposing those bounds.

A wide metabolic matrix supplies many reaction controls for comparatively few pools. For mm retained concentrations and n>mn>m reaction fluxes, S∈Rm×nS\in\mathbb R^{m\times n} has more columns than rows. This makes full row rank a natural case to examine: the reaction columns span all retained concentration directions. In that case, choosing fluxes lets us assign every concentration derivative independently.8

Full row rank lets the free-flux model follow a prescribed concentration trajectory. Choose a differentiable, nonnegative q(t)q(t) with the specified initial condition. At each time, solve

Sv(t)=q˙(t)−Sww(t).S v(t)=\dot q(t)-S^w w(t).

A solution exists for every right-hand side when rank⁡S=m\operatorname{rank}S=m. The fluxes can therefore realize the requested trajectory, including perfect compensation of a changing demand. The relaxed model has replaced the metabolic response with independently adjustable inputs.

Our two-reaction model shows exactly what is lost. Solving its balance for the two fluxes gives

v1=2q˙I+q˙ATP+w,v2=q˙I+q˙ATP+w.v_1=2\dot q_I+\dot q_{\mathrm{ATP}}+w,\qquad v_2=\dot q_I+\dot q_{\mathrm{ATP}}+w.

Whenever these values satisfy the flux bounds, the relaxation can produce the requested differentiable pool trajectory. In particular, it can keep both pools perfectly constant through a demand change simply by setting v1(t)=v2(t)=w(t)v_1(t)=v_2(t)=w(t) instantly. The ATP investment difficulty has disappeared because we discarded the dependence of reaction rates on ATP and intermediate concentrations.

Independent protein production and degradation make the control freedom explicit

Each protein has a production flux and a degradation flux in a projected gene-expression model. Retain only the mm protein concentrations. Production adds one unit to its protein pool. Degradation removes one unit from that pool. Other protein pools are unchanged. Order the production columns first and the degradation columns second. Then

S=[Im  −Im],q˙=vprod−vdeg,rank⁡S=m.S=[I_m\; -I_m],\qquad\dot q=v^{\mathrm{prod}}-v^{\mathrm{deg}},\qquad\operatorname{rank}S=m.

Here ImI_m is the identity matrix. For two proteins, the columns are production of protein 1, production of protein 2, degradation of protein 1 and degradation of protein 2:

S=(10−10010−1).S=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&-1&0\\0&1&0&-1\end{pmatrix}.

Even nonnegative fluxes can realize every requested derivative. For any differentiable, nonnegative protein trajectory with the given initial condition, choose the production and degradation fluxes component by component:

viprod(t)=max⁡{q˙i(t),0},videg(t)=max⁡{−q˙i(t),0}.v_i^{\mathrm{prod}}(t)=\max\{\dot q_i(t),0\},\qquad v_i^{\mathrm{deg}}(t)=\max\{-\dot q_i(t),0\}.

Their difference is exactly q˙i(t)\dot q_i(t). Thus the free-flux model can prescribe all protein concentrations independently. Translation capacity, degradation kinetics and shared resources are the biological structure that this projection has relaxed.

The control freedom explains why stoichiometry alone can leave dynamics underdetermined. Sign and capacity bounds can limit which trajectories remain feasible. Kinetic and regulatory relations determine how the fluxes actually respond to the concentrations. The useful next question is what the retained accounting and resource bounds can establish at steady state.

Change the question to sustained output at steady internal pools

Steady performance is a distinct task. We now ask what production can be sustained with approximately constant retained internal pools. Setting accumulation to zero selects this task. It is not a relaxation of all possible transient histories. Relaxing kinetic restrictions within the steady task gives the flux balance problem:

Sv+Sww=0,max⁡v cTvsubject to the balance and flux bounds.\boxed{S v+S^w w=0,\qquad\max_v\ c^{\mathsf T}v\quad\text{subject to the balance and flux bounds}.}

The vector cc selects the valued output, such as biomass production. This linear program is flux balance analysis. Nonzero fluxes can pass through steady pools. The calculation neither supplies their concentrations nor proves that a kinetic steady state is stable.2

First specify behavior through an objective and biochemical constraints. Then state which constraints a tractable approximation relaxes and what its solution can establish.

Optional · Specify complex behavior through goals, constraints and architecture

A compact specification can describe a complicated behavior. The main lecture uses this idea to formulate metabolism. This extension develops the broader connection to machine design. It is outside the 95-minute teaching route.

Follow one question through four settings: what must we specify before the desired behavior can be found? First organize a machine into modules. Then solve the same spring carriage as a static system, a dynamical system and a controlled system. Finally compare mechanical variational principles and learning from examples.

Specify each module's task, interfaces and physical limits

Hierarchy lets us reason at the resolution of the task. A module receives inputs and produces outputs. Its specification states the relationship it should achieve, the conditions it assumes and the limits it must respect. We can then combine modules through those interfaces without writing every microscopic state into every calculation. Planning, feedback and fast physical actuation often occupy different levels of this architecture.16

Machine and taskModule responsibilitiesConstraints at the interfaces
Crane: place a load at a destinationA planner chooses a path. Feedback tracks motion and limits load sway. Motors produce the requested forces.Rope tension, allowable sway, motor torque, structural load, collision clearance and available power.
Car: follow a safe routeA planner chooses a path and speed. Steering and braking track them. Tires and power electronics transmit the physical action.Road friction, stopping distance, steering limits, battery or fuel supply and actuator response time.
Computer: execute a program correctlyThe program specifies a computation. A scheduler assigns resources. Instructions organize circuit operations.Instruction semantics, memory capacity, timing, communication bandwidth, power and temperature.

The interfaces determine whether the pieces can achieve the overall task together. A crane planner cannot request motion faster than the sway controller and motors can realize. Two computer tasks cannot each assume exclusive access to the same finite memory. Shared resources and response times couple the modules. Those couplings must appear in the architecture's constraints.

An optimization can turn the specification into a design or a prediction. A crane planner might minimize travel time subject to a sway limit. A scheduler might minimize delay subject to resource and correctness constraints. A metabolic model might maximize growth subject to chemical balance and enzyme capacity. The modules need not solve these problems online. Their design can implement a policy found beforehand.

Three uses of optimization will appear below. An optimization can reformulate known physics, design an action from a goal, or fit a model to observations. Each use gains clarity from a stated objective and constraints. The physical or empirical justification for the objective differs across the three.

Three solved descriptions: equilibrium, motion and feedback control

One spring carriage makes the alternative descriptions concrete. A carriage moves along a rail with position 0≤x≤L0\leq x\leq L. Its spring pulls toward x=0x=0 with stiffness ksk_s. A load applies force FloadF_{\mathrm{load}}. Viscous drag has coefficient cdragc_{\mathrm{drag}}. We neglect inertia. Use ks=4 N/mk_s=4\,\mathrm{N/m}, cdrag=2 N s/mc_{\mathrm{drag}}=2\,\mathrm{N\,s/m} and L=1 mL=1\,\mathrm m. These are illustrative mechanical parameters.

1. A static input-output function from constrained energy minimization

Force balance gives the equilibrium directly. Away from the stops, ksx=Floadk_sx=F_{\mathrm{load}}. A stop supplies a contact force when that balance would put the carriage outside the rail. The resulting input-output function is

x∗(Fload)=clip⁡ ⁣(Floadks,0,L).x^*(F_{\mathrm{load}})=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{F_{\mathrm{load}}}{k_s},0,L\right).

Here clip⁡(z,a,b)=min⁡{b,max⁡{a,z}}\operatorname{clip}(z,a,b)=\min\{b,\max\{a,z\}\} truncates a number to the interval [a,b][a,b].

The same equilibrium minimizes the physical potential energy. The spring stores energy and the applied load does work. Their potential is E(x)=ksx2/2−FloadxE(x)=k_sx^2/2-F_{\mathrm{load}}x, in joules. Therefore

x∗∈argmin⁡0≤x≤L E(x).x^*\in\underset{0\leq x\leq L}{\operatorname{argmin}}\ E(x).

Strict convexity makes the minimizer unique. Differentiation gives the interior force balance. The inequality constraints supply the two possible contact forces. The objective is a physical energy, not a distance to a previously calculated answer.

2. A trajectory from a sequence of state-dependent minimizations

Drag prevents the carriage from jumping to each new equilibrium. In the rail's interior, the direct equation is cdragx˙=Fload−ksxc_{\mathrm{drag}}\dot x=F_{\mathrm{load}}-k_sx. For a constant load whose equilibrium lies inside the rail,

x(t)=Floadks+[x(0)−Floadks]e−kst/cdrag.x(t)=\frac{F_{\mathrm{load}}}{k_s}+\left[x(0)-\frac{F_{\mathrm{load}}}{k_s}\right]e^{-k_st/c_{\mathrm{drag}}}.

A minimum over instantaneous velocities describes the same overdamped motion. At the current position, let vv be a candidate velocity. Minimize half the viscous dissipation plus the rate of change of potential energy. [18, §2]

x˙=argmin⁡v∈T(x)[cdrag2v2+(ksx−Fload)v].\dot x=\underset{v\in T(x)}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left[\frac{c_{\mathrm{drag}}}{2}v^2+(k_sx-F_{\mathrm{load}})v\right].

The objective has units of power. The admissible velocity set T(x)T(x) is all real velocities inside the rail, nonnegative velocities at x=0x=0, and nonpositive velocities at x=Lx=L. Differentiating the interior objective recovers the force law with drag. At a stop, the constraint prevents motion through the stop.

A time-discrete version makes the retained memory explicit. Given the current position xnx_n and a time step Δt>0\Delta t>0, use

xn+1=argmin⁡0≤z≤L[cdrag2Δt(z−xn)2+E(z)].x_{n+1}=\underset{0\leq z\leq L}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left[\frac{c_{\mathrm{drag}}}{2\Delta t}(z-x_n)^2+E(z)\right].
xn+1=clip⁡ ⁣(cdragxn+ΔtFloadcdrag+ksΔt,0,L).x_{n+1}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{c_{\mathrm{drag}}x_n+\Delta t F_{\mathrm{load}}}{c_{\mathrm{drag}}+k_s\Delta t},0,L\right).

This is a backward-Euler approximation. It approaches the continuous dynamics as the time step decreases. The previous position remains in every minimization. Minimizing EE alone at every instant would discard the transient.

3. A feedback law synthesized from a convergence goal and a motor limit

Now add a motor and ask for a specified response. The motor force uu satisfies ∣u∣≤U|u|\leq U, and the plant obeys cdragx˙=Fload−ksx+uc_{\mathrm{drag}}\dot x=F_{\mathrm{load}}-k_sx+u in the interior. Choose target r∈(0,L)r\in(0,L), position error e=x−re=x-r and desired decay rate λ>0\lambda>0. The holding force uhold=ksr−Floadu_{\mathrm{hold}}=k_sr-F_{\mathrm{load}} must satisfy ∣uhold∣≤U|u_{\mathrm{hold}}|\leq U.

A control Lyapunov function specifies a goal while retaining the plant dynamics. Let a known plant have state vector zz, input uu and dynamics z˙=f(z,u)\dot z=f(z,u). A control Lyapunov function V(z)V(z) is zero at the target and positive away from it. Over the stated operating region, an admissible input can make V˙=∇V⋅f(z,u)\dot V=\nabla V\cdot f(z,u) negative at every other state. An optimization selects an input by imposing the desired decrease as a constraint. The plant law determines which inputs can meet that constraint. [19, §IIA–C]

For the carriage, a quadratic function gives an explicit decrease constraint. Let V=e2/2V=e^2/2. During any interval on which V˙≤−2λV\dot V\leq-2\lambda V is feasible and enforced, the position error decays at least at rate λ\lambda. Substituting the plant gives the controller optimization:

minimize⁡∣u∣≤U 12(u−uhold)2\underset{|u|\leq U}{\operatorname{minimize}}\ \frac12(u-u_{\mathrm{hold}})^2
subject toe(Fload−ksx+u)≤−cdragλe2.\text{subject to}\quad e(F_{\mathrm{load}}-k_sx+u)\leq-c_{\mathrm{drag}}\lambda e^2.

The solution distinguishes a sufficient natural response from extra force correction. Define β=max⁡(cdragλ−ks,0)\beta=\max(c_{\mathrm{drag}}\lambda-k_s,0), in newtons per metre. When the requested decrease is feasible, the optimizer is u=uhold−βeu=u_{\mathrm{hold}}-\beta e. If λ≤ks/cdrag\lambda\leq k_s/c_{\mathrm{drag}}, the spring's natural convergence already meets the goal and u=uholdu=u_{\mathrm{hold}} costs no additional correction.

For β>0\beta>0, the requested rate is feasible precisely at positions satisfying

r−U−uholdβ≤x≤r+U+uholdβ,0≤x≤L.r-\frac{U-u_{\mathrm{hold}}}{\beta}\leq x\leq r+\frac{U+u_{\mathrm{hold}}}{\beta},\qquad 0\leq x\leq L.

When the motor cannot meet that rate, make the shortfall explicit. Add a nonnegative slack ss to the right side of the decrease inequality. First minimize ss. Among the minimum-slack choices, minimize the squared force correction. This declared priority yields

u∗(x)=clip⁡ ⁣[uhold−β(x−r),−U,U].u^*(x)=\operatorname{clip}\!\left[u_{\mathrm{hold}}-\beta(x-r),-U,U\right].

The minimum slack is s∗=max⁡{0,e(Fload−ksx+u∗)+cdragλe2}s^*=\max\{0,e(F_{\mathrm{load}}-k_sx+u^*)+c_{\mathrm{drag}}\lambda e^2\}, in newton metres. A positive slack says that the requested convergence rate is temporarily unattainable. It does not claim the position target is unreachable.

Compare the three descriptions on the same carriage. The static stage varies the load. The dynamic stage starts at x(0)=0.25 mx(0)=0.25\,\mathrm m. The control stage uses Fload=1 NF_{\mathrm{load}}=1\,\mathrm N, r=0.75 mr=0.75\,\mathrm m, U=3 NU=3\,\mathrm N and the same initial position.

The strongest request has a calculable period of saturation. For λ=4 s−1\lambda=4\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}, the requested rate is feasible only when x≥0.5 mx\geq0.5\,\mathrm m. Initially the motor supplies its maximum 3 N3\,\mathrm N. The carriage reaches that feasible interval at tswitch=(0.5 s)ln⁡(3/2)≈0.203 st_{\mathrm{switch}}=(0.5\,\mathrm s)\ln(3/2)\approx0.203\,\mathrm s. The exact continuous response is

x(t)={1 m−(0.75 m)e−(2 s−1)t,0≤t≤tswitch,0.75 m−(0.25 m)e−(4 s−1)(t−tswitch),t≥tswitch.x(t)=\begin{cases}1\,\mathrm m-(0.75\,\mathrm m)e^{-(2\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})t},&0\leq t\leq t_{\mathrm{switch}},\\0.75\,\mathrm m-(0.25\,\mathrm m)e^{-(4\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})(t-t_{\mathrm{switch}})},&t\geq t_{\mathrm{switch}}.\end{cases}

Time 0.00 s. Position 0.250 m. Motor 3.000 N. Minimum constraint slack 0.500 N m. The requested rate exceeds the available motor force here.

Play starts motion only on request. The slider works without animation. Scroll the diagrams sideways on narrow screens. Solid curves are continuous predictions. Dots in the dynamic stage are backward-Euler steps of 0.25 s.

The three optimization statements have different scientific roles. Energy minimization and velocity minimization reformulate the specified spring and drag physics. The controller optimization adds a desired rate, a motor limit and a priority for allocating effort. It synthesizes a new feedback law. Metabolic optimization needs the same distinction: which restrictions describe physical possibilities, and which objective proposes how the cell selects among them?

Use generalized coordinates to organize a crane's mechanics

A variational formulation can remove internal constraint forces from the calculation. Consider a trolley of mass MM carrying a point load of mass mm on a rigid, massless link of length ℓ\ell. A taut rope has the same kinematics while its tension stays positive. Let XX be trolley position and θ\theta the load angle from downward vertical. The load coordinates are

xload=X+ℓsin⁡θ,yload=−ℓcos⁡θ.x_{\mathrm{load}}=X+\ell\sin\theta,\qquad y_{\mathrm{load}}=-\ell\cos\theta.

These coordinates enforce the fixed-length constraint. Newton's equations in Cartesian coordinates would include the link force and the length constraint. The generalized coordinates (X,θ)(X,\theta) let us work directly with the two independent motions.

Kinetic and potential energy assemble the coupled dynamics. Let gg denote gravitational acceleration. Neglect friction and link mass. The total kinetic energy KK, gravitational potential energy EgravE_{\mathrm{grav}} and Lagrangian L\mathcal L are

K=12(M+m)X˙2+mℓX˙θ˙cos⁡θ+12mℓ2θ˙2,Egrav=mgℓ(1−cos⁡θ),L=K−Egrav.\begin{aligned} K&=\tfrac12(M+m)\dot X^2+m\ell\dot X\dot\theta\cos\theta+\tfrac12m\ell^2\dot\theta^2,\\ E_{\mathrm{grav}}&=mg\ell(1-\cos\theta),\qquad \mathcal L=K-E_{\mathrm{grav}}. \end{aligned}

Stationary action yields the unforced trajectory equations. For a history between fixed endpoint configurations at times t0t_0 and t1t_1, define the action A=∫t0t1L dt\mathcal A=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\mathcal L\,dt. Requiring its first variation to vanish gives the Euler–Lagrange equations. The action is stationary. It need not be a minimum over the interval under consideration.17

An applied trolley force enters as a generalized force. Write that force as FmotorF_{\mathrm{motor}}. The force acts on XX, and there is no independent applied torque on θ\theta. The forced Euler–Lagrange equations become

ddt∂L∂X˙−∂L∂X=Fmotor,ddt∂L∂θ˙−∂L∂θ=0.\begin{aligned} \frac d{dt}\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\dot X}-\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial X}&=F_{\mathrm{motor}},\\ \frac d{dt}\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\dot\theta}-\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\theta}&=0. \end{aligned}

Taking the derivatives gives the two coupled equations without solving for the internal link force:

(M+m)X¨+mℓ(θ¨cos⁡θ−θ˙2sin⁡θ)=Fmotor,ℓθ¨+X¨cos⁡θ+gsin⁡θ=0.\begin{aligned} (M+m)\ddot X+m\ell(\ddot\theta\cos\theta-\dot\theta^2\sin\theta)&=F_{\mathrm{motor}},\\ \ell\ddot\theta+\ddot X\cos\theta+g\sin\theta&=0. \end{aligned}

The variational principle organizes the same mechanical laws. It makes constraints and coupling easier to handle as mechanisms become more complicated. It does not assert that the crane chooses the fastest or safest route. Those are separate design objectives. To select a route, we can optimize a travel or energy cost subject to these dynamics, endpoint requirements, clearance and actuator bounds. The physical variational principle supplies the plant. The design optimization selects its operation.

Learn visual features by optimizing a training objective

Learning lets examples specify a recognition task whose rules are difficult to write directly. A hand-designed vision system chooses image measurements and rules for combining them. A neural network instead has adjustable transformations whose parameters are trained jointly. Early convolutional systems demonstrated how task-dependent features could be learned from images through gradient-based training.20

A layered architecture defines which functions can be learned. Let an image be II, and set its first representation to h0=Ih_0=I. A simple layer computes hj+1=σj(Wjhj+bj)h_{j+1}=\sigma_j(W_jh_j+b_j). The matrices or convolution operators WjW_j and offsets bjb_j are learned. The functions σj\sigma_j and the pattern of connections are architectural choices. The resulting network gives class probabilities pθ(y∣I)p_\theta(y\mid I), where θ\theta collects its trainable parameters.

The training objective states what the parameters should achieve on examples. Given NN labeled images (Ii,yi)(I_i,y_i), a common formulation minimizes the average negative log probability of the correct class plus a regularization cost:

min⁡θ∈Θ 1N∑i=1N−log⁡pθ(yi∣Ii)+λregR(θ).\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\ \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}-\log p_\theta(y_i\mid I_i)+\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}R(\theta).

The set Θ\Theta contains the parameters permitted by the architecture and any hard restrictions. The function RR penalizes selected parameter properties, and λreg≥0\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}\geq0 weights that penalty. Intermediate representations change during training because they affect the final task loss. We need not prescribe every feature that distinguishes a face, vehicle or animal.

Computation makes a compact task specification usable at scale. Large image datasets, GPU computation and optimization enabled much larger learned models, as the ImageNet convolutional-network study illustrates. The optimization is generally nonconvex. Data, architecture, initialization and the training algorithm all affect the result.21

Training and prediction use the learned model differently. Training adjusts θ\theta to reduce the stated objective. Ordinary inference then evaluates pθ(y∣I)p_\theta(y\mid I) with the trained parameters fixed. A small training loss alone does not establish performance on new images. Held-out evaluation and the relation between training and use conditions remain essential.

The shared idea is to specify success before constructing the detailed response. A learning objective selects a function from a model class. A control objective selects actions allowed by a plant. A metabolic objective selects behavior allowed by biochemical machinery. In each case, we must justify the chosen task and the permitted choices.

State which feature of the behavior a relaxation bounds

An upper bound on one score does not determine a unique trajectory. Two ATP histories can have the same cumulative production but different minimum ATP levels. If the question concerns ATP at a specified time t∗t_*, define the observable ϕ[q,v]=qATP(t∗)\phi[q,v]=q_{\mathrm{ATP}}(t_*). For an actual history in the biochemical feasible set and any outer relaxation Crelaxed\mathcal C_{\mathrm{relaxed}},

inf⁡(q,v)∈Crelaxedϕ[q,v] ≤ ϕ[qactual,vactual] ≤ sup⁡(q,v)∈Crelaxedϕ[q,v].\inf_{(q,v)\in\mathcal C_{\mathrm{relaxed}}}\phi[q,v]\ \leq\ \phi[q_{\mathrm{actual}},v_{\mathrm{actual}}]\ \leq\ \sup_{(q,v)\in\mathcal C_{\mathrm{relaxed}}}\phi[q,v].

Repeating this calculation over times gives an envelope containing every permitted ATP trajectory. Extremes at different times can come from different histories. The upper edge of the envelope need not itself be one possible trajectory. More retained biochemical constraints can tighten these bounds.

The information available to a controller is also a constraint. An offline plan may use a known future demand history. A feedback policy must act from the observations available at that time. To interpret an optimized metabolic trajectory as feedback behavior, include those information restrictions and any controller memory in the admissible family.

A bound also needs a valid optimization certificate. A global maximum over a larger set gives the stated upper bound. A feasible point found by a local maximization algorithm only gives a candidate score. Linear programming, convex formulations and suitable dual bounds can provide certificates where available. This is why the linear flux balance calculation and the local nonlinear control calculations in Part 3 carry different claims.15

Return to metabolism with three explicit choices. State the function to be achieved, the biochemical behavior permitted and the mathematical guarantee supplied by the calculation. This makes both a detailed prediction and a coarse performance bound interpretable.

5Solve the glycolysis balance before scaling up

The same ATP-investment pathway lets us solve a flux balance analysis problem by hand. First ATP demand fixes both pathway fluxes. Then a growth branch creates a choice that an uptake bound and an objective resolve. This sequence follows the lecturer’s constraint-based modeling slides.7

The two-reaction steady state is a square matrix problem. Write the ATP investment coefficient as ν>0\nu>0. Setting the pool derivatives to zero moves the imposed ATP demand to the right-hand side:

(1−1−νν+1)⏟S(v1v2)=(0w).\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-\nu&\nu+1\end{pmatrix}}_{S}\begin{pmatrix}v_1\\v_2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\w\end{pmatrix}.

Matrix inversion gives the unique fluxes needed to meet that demand. The determinant is (ν+1)−ν=1(\nu+1)-\nu=1, so

S−1=(ν+11ν1),(v1v2)=S−1(0w)=(ww).S^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\nu+1&1\\\nu&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\begin{pmatrix}v_1\\v_2\end{pmatrix}=S^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\w\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}w\\w\end{pmatrix}.

For example, an ATP draw of one flux unit requires one unit through each pathway reaction. There is no internal flux choice left for an objective to select.

The same steady fluxes are compatible with stable or oscillatory rate laws. ATP investment matters during the transient even though ν\nu cancels from this balance.

Adding growth makes an ATP-allocation decision possible. Introduce a third flux vgrow≥0v_{\mathrm{grow}}\geq0 that allocates ATP to biosynthesis. In this projected teaching model, growth consumes one ATP unit and no retained intermediate. It is an energy-allocation proxy. A specific growth rate requires biomass composition and a mass normalization. The complete network retains the ATP investment/payoff loop. Maintenance and growth are separate outlets from its ATP pool.

P5Steady balance gives the allocation relation. A resource bound makes its optimum finite.

(q˙Iq˙ATP)=(1−10−νν+1−1)(v1v2vgrow)+(0−1)w.\begin{pmatrix}\dot q_I\\\dot q_{\mathrm{ATP}}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\-\nu&\nu+1&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}v_1\\v_2\\v_{\mathrm{grow}}\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0\\-1\end{pmatrix}w.

Three reaction fluxes now satisfy only two pool balances. The two rows are independent, so one free coefficient remains. We need the whole solution space before choosing an optimum. At ν=1\nu=1, the steady equation and its Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse are

Sv=(0w),S=(1−10−12−1),S†=(11/301/3−1−2/3).S v=\begin{pmatrix}0\\w\end{pmatrix},\qquad S=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S^{\dagger}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/3\\0&1/3\\-1&-2/3\end{pmatrix}.

The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse gives one solution, and the null space gives every allowed adjustment. Multiplying by S†S^{\dagger} gives the particular solution (w/3,w/3,−2w/3)T(w/3,w/3,-2w/3)^{\mathsf T}. The vector (1,1,1)T(1,1,1)^{\mathsf T} lies in the null space of SS. It adds the same throughput to investment, payoff and growth without changing either pool balance. Hence every solution has the form

v=w3(11−2)+α(111),α∈R.\boxed{v=\frac{w}{3}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\alpha\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\alpha\in\mathbb R.}

The scalar α\alpha has flux units. The particular solution is an algebraic starting point. For positive demand, its negative growth entry is not a feasible allocation. Nonnegative growth requires α≥2w/3\alpha\geq2w/3.

Using growth itself as the coefficient makes the allocation easy to read. Since vgrow=α−2w/3v_{\mathrm{grow}}=\alpha-2w/3, the same solution space becomes

(v1v2vgrow)=w(110)+vgrow(111).\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}v_1\\v_2\\v_{\mathrm{grow}}\end{pmatrix}=w\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+v_{\mathrm{grow}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}.}

The first term supplies the external ATP draw. The second term sends each extra unit of growth through one additional unit of investment and payoff. The growth flux is still a choice, rather than an optimum.

There is no finite maximum growth flux until a resource or capacity is bounded. Let UU be the upstream supply limit, so that 0≤v1≤U0\leq v_1\leq U. Substituting v1=w+vgrowv_1=w+v_{\mathrm{grow}} gives the feasible interval

2w3≤α≤U−w3,0≤vgrow≤U−w.\frac{2w}{3}\leq\alpha\leq U-\frac{w}{3},\qquad 0\leq v_{\mathrm{grow}}\leq U-w.

Maximizing the growth flux selects the upper endpoint when U≥wU\geq w:

v∗=(U,U,U−w)T.\boxed{v^*=(U,U,U-w)^{\mathsf T}.}

At U=wU=w, maintenance uses all available supply. At U<wU<w, even zero growth cannot give a feasible nonnegative steady flux. For w=1w=1 and U=3U=3, the vectors (1,1,0)(1,1,0), (2,2,1)(2,2,1) and (3,3,2)(3,3,2) all balance. The last one maximizes growth.

An explicit glucose pool uses the declared throughput convention. Let qGlcq_{\mathrm{Glc}} be actual glucose concentration and wGlcw_{\mathrm{Glc}} its import flux. Each investment event consumes half a glucose, so q˙Glc=wGlc−v1/2\dot q_{\mathrm{Glc}}=w_{\mathrm{Glc}}-v_1/2. At steady state, fixed import gives v1=v2=2wGlcv_1=v_2=2w_{\mathrm{Glc}} and vgrow=2wGlc−wv_{\mathrm{grow}}=2w_{\mathrm{Glc}}-w. An uptake capacity limits import without requiring it to equal the cap.

Use a matrix inverse when the steady flux is unique. Use a particular solution and null-space coefficients when internal allocations remain free. Bounds and an objective then select among those allocations.

6Apply the same optimization to an E. coli reconstruction

With the same glucose supply, how much does access to oxygen change the growth ceiling? Glucose supplies building material and chemical energy. Oxygen changes which ATP-producing routes are available. To account for these coupled pathways, we use iJO1366, a genome-scale reconstruction of Escherichia coli K-12 MG1655.

A reconstruction turns many known reactions into one balance matrix. The archived iJO1366 model has 1,805 rows for compartment-indexed metabolite pools and 2,583 columns for flux variables. Most entries are zero because each reaction changes only a few pools. A phosphofructokinase column gives a concrete ATP-investing step: one unit of flux consumes one ATP and one fructose 6-phosphate while producing ADP, fructose 1,6-bisphosphate and a proton. Every other reaction contributes its own column.4, 5

Replace the teaching growth sink with a biomass recipe. The small example allocated ATP to a single growth branch. A reconstruction specifies how much of many precursors is needed to make a unit of biomass. Let μ\mu be its specific growth rate, in inverse hours. Increasing the biomass flux increases every one of these demands together. Balance requires the rest of the network to replenish them.

P6The same balance becomes a computable organism-scale performance bound.

The objective is the model's core biomass reaction. Its fixed composition converts the biomass flux into a specific growth rate μ\mu, in inverse hours. All internal balances and archived bounds remain active. Here exchange fluxes join the other columns in vv, so the balance is written Sv=0Sv=0.

Growth requires a convention for the steady-pool approximation. A concentration balance in a growing volume includes dilution, −μq-\mu q. FBA neglects dilution of the retained metabolite pools relative to their turnover while keeping incorporation into biomass as an explicit sink. Lecture 14 will account for production and dilution together.

Model counts and the meaning of the core biomass objective

The executable file includes exchange, biomass and compartment-indexed pools. The 2011 paper instead reports 1,366 biological genes, 2,251 metabolic and transport reactions and 1,136 unique metabolites. The different counts describe different objects.

The word “core” names one biomass composition inside iJO1366. It does not mean the separate 95-reaction E. coli core teaching model.

The environment enters through exchange bounds. A negative exchange flux denotes import. We change the glucose uptake cap GG and oxygen uptake cap OO while retaining the archived medium and ATP-maintenance requirement:

−G≤vEX,glucose≤1000,−O≤vEX,oxygen≤1000,vATPM≥3.15.-G\leq v_{\mathrm{EX,glucose}}\leq1000,\qquad-O\leq v_{\mathrm{EX,oxygen}}\leq1000,\qquad v_{\mathrm{ATPM}}\geq3.15.

These fluxes are in millimoles per gram dry weight per hour. The large upper bounds are modeling bounds, not measured enzyme capacities. The exchange constraints limit supply. They do not force the model to consume all available oxygen.

Use the controls to compare constraints, one at a time. Keep the glucose uptake cap at 10. Compare oxygen caps 0, 5 and 20 using the three buttons. Track the growth bound and the products exported by the selected solution. Then increase the oxygen cap from 20 to 30. Predict whether relaxing this one constraint can ever lower the best attainable growth.

Relaxing one bound preserves every previously feasible solution. With the same glucose cap and objective, increasing the oxygen cap can therefore only increase or preserve the maximal growth rate. At glucose cap 10, the bound is approximately 0.242, 0.492 and 0.982 per hour for oxygen caps 0, 5 and 20. The computation gives a numerical instance of the nested-set argument.

A flat oxygen curve does not mean every growth constraint has disappeared. At glucose cap 10, raising the oxygen cap from 20 to 30 gives the same growth bound. Keep oxygen at 20 and raise the glucose cap to 20 instead. The bound rises from 0.982 to 1.455 per hour. The effect of a constraint depends on which other supplies remain limited.

The selected solution also allocates uptake and export. At glucose cap 10 and oxygen cap 5, the selected solution secretes acetate, ethanol and formate. At oxygen cap 20, the selected solution uses about 17.58 oxygen units and secretes none of these three products. A single optimal internal flux pattern need not be unique. Minimizing and maximizing individual fluxes while holding growth optimal reveals that remaining freedom.

Inspect all 2,583 reaction records and three computed conditions

The searchable table shows each complete signed stoichiometric column, gene rule and original bounds. Flux columns use glucose cap 10 and oxygen caps 0, 5 and 20. They are minimum-total-flux representatives at maximal growth. Start by finding PFK to inspect the five coefficients shown in Figure 6 and its gene rule. Then find BIOMASS to inspect the larger recipe. Gene associations identify possible enzymes. They do not supply enzyme concentrations or kinetic laws.

ReactionOriginal boundsOxygen 0Oxygen 5Oxygen 20
Compare with the 2022 notebook's smaller teaching model

The preserved notebook first loads iJO1366, then replaces it with the COBRA textbook model. That 95-reaction model is valuable for inspecting central metabolism. It is not a genome-scale model. The updated calculation retains both versions. With glucose cap 10 and oxygen cap 20, the core teaching model predicts 0.833 h−10.833\,\mathrm{h}^{-1}. Its ATP-maintenance lower bound is 8.39 rather than 3.15. Numerical answers should always be tied to a named model, objective and medium.

Genome-scale reconstruction grew through sequencing and biochemical curation. The first genome-scale E. coli reconstruction was assembled in 2000. iJO1366 is a later curated version of that lineage. Such reconstructions provide metabolic constraints for broader virtual-cell models. They do not by themselves specify every cellular behavior.4

The reconstruction bounds steady metabolic capabilities, rather than all cell behaviors. A biomass objective does not model sensing, enzyme adjustment or the transition into growth arrest. One dynamic extension couples repeated steady-state optimizations to extracellular nutrient and biomass dynamics while keeping internal pools quasi-steady. That construction does not resolve the intracellular ATP transient.

A dynamic prediction depends on which pools and rate dependencies are retained. More general dynamic flux balance analysis formulations optimize concentration and flux trajectories and can include kinetic constraints. For our glycolytic question, we need the internal ATP and intermediate dynamics together with restrictions on how their reaction rates respond.9

Specify the reconstruction, biomass objective, medium and exchange limits before quoting a growth prediction. A genome-scale steady-state calculation still leaves intracellular regulation and transients to be explained.

The steady calculation cannot recover the glycolytic oscillation. Which biochemical constraints did we leave out?

Part 3 · Restore binding and catalysis to predict metabolic dynamics

Change what the optimizer controls. Keep the catalytic dependence on the pools that the cell must regulate.

7Binding restricts how regulation can change catalytic fluxes

We do know more than the stoichiometric matrix. A cell changes metabolic rates through molecular interactions with enzymes. Flux exponent control retains this additional structure without specifying every regulatory mechanism.

Enzymes keep catalyzing when their regulation is held fixed. In glycolysis, fixing an enzyme's activity does not fix its flux. The investment rate still depends on ATP. The payoff rate still depends on intermediate. We should therefore place these concentration dependences inside the plant and let the unknown regulation act on enzyme activity.

P7Keep substrate-dependent catalysis in the plant. Constrain the unknown regulation using what binding can implement.

The binding-catalysis split distinguishes two sources of change. Binding redistributes molecules among free and complexed states. Catalysis changes molecular totals. On a fast metabolic timescale, enzyme totals may be held fixed while binding changes their active fractions. On a longer timescale, enzyme synthesis, degradation and growth dilution must become part of the dynamics. Covalent enzyme modification also requires catalytic state-changing reactions. The relevant molecular steps determine the model boundary.1

First keep the catalytic dependence that remains when enzyme activity is fixed. For our glycolysis example, remove the specified Hill denominators and retain their positive activity factors as controls:

vˉ1=2qˉATPu1,vˉ2=2κqˉIu2,dqˉdtˉ=Svˉ(qˉ,u)+Swwˉ.\bar v_1=2\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}u_1,\qquad\bar v_2=2\kappa\bar q_Iu_2,\qquad\frac{d\bar q}{d\bar t}=S\bar v(\bar q,u)+S^w\bar w.

Substituting the earlier Hill factors recovers the known model. Fixing activity still leaves flux dependent on ATP or intermediate. The unknown regulation acts on this catalytic plant.

The same activity can conceal different feedback responses. In every Hill example, the baseline ATP level is one and the upstream activity is u1∗=1/2u_1^*=1/2. The upstream flux is therefore one for every hh. What differs is how activity changes when ATP changes. We need a measure of that response, not just its value at one operating point.

The reaction order measures the relative response of flux to concentration. For a static regulatory law u1=u1(qˉATP)u_1=u_1(\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}), the resulting upstream flux depends on ATP alone. Define its ATP reaction order aa at the baseline by

a=dlog⁡vˉ1dlog⁡qˉATP=1+dlog⁡u1dlog⁡qˉATP.a=\frac{d\log\bar v_1}{d\log\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}}=1+\frac{d\log u_1}{d\log\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}}.

A small one-percent ATP increase produces approximately an aa-percent flux change, with other independent quantities held fixed. The explicit ATP substrate factor contributes one. The regulatory response supplies the remaining slope. For the Hill law, the activity slope at baseline is −h-h, so a=1−ha=1-h.

A binding mechanism restricts which slopes can occur. Consider productive binding E+ATP⇌k−k+C→kcatE+productsE+\mathrm{ATP}\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{k_+}C\xrightarrow{k_{\mathrm{cat}}}E+\text{products}. Here CC is the enzyme–ATP complex. Hold other required substrates fixed. Assume fast binding equilibrium, fixed enzyme total qEq_E and negligible ATP depletion by a trace enzyme, so free ATP approximates qATPq_{\mathrm{ATP}}. With Kd=k−/k+K_d=k_-/k_+,

v1=kcatqEqATPKd+qATP,a=KdKd+qATP∈(0,1).v_1=k_{\mathrm{cat}}q_E\frac{q_{\mathrm{ATP}}}{K_d+q_{\mathrm{ATP}}},\qquad a=\frac{K_d}{K_d+q_{\mathrm{ATP}}}\in(0,1).

In the multiplicative representation, the activity factor is proportional to the free-enzyme fraction, u1∝1/(1+qATP/Kd)u_1\propto1/(1+q_{\mathrm{ATP}}/K_d). Its logarithmic slope is a−1a-1. Binding lowers the flux reaction order from one toward zero without reversing its sign. A negative flux reaction order requires additional regulation, such as ATP binding that inhibits enzyme activity.

Now ask which orders stabilize the same glycolysis operating point. Keep upstream flux independent of intermediate and payoff first order in intermediate. For a static downstream regulatory law, let b=∂log⁡vˉ2/∂log⁡qˉATPb=\partial\log\bar v_2/\partial\log\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}} be the downstream ATP reaction order after substituting that law, with intermediate held fixed. The earlier Hill law gives b=−g=−0.3b=-g=-0.3 at baseline. Insert these slopes into the two concentration balances. The local stability test gives

2b−κ<a<0,hence−1.7<a<0for κ=1.1.\boxed{2b-\kappa<a<0,\qquad\text{hence}\quad-1.7<a<0\quad\text{for }\kappa=1.1.}

A3 gives the two-by-two calculation. The strict inequalities exclude marginal linearizations at the two endpoints. The comparison holds the external demand fixed and asks whether small pool perturbations decay.

The binding restriction now rules out a proposed controller. Even after choosing the rate prefactor to match the baseline flux, productive ATP binding leaves a positive reaction order. Its allowed orders do not intersect the negative interval required for stability. The running Hill examples supply inhibitory regulation instead. Their orders are −1.5,−1.8,−2.1-1.5,-1.8,-2.1. The first lies inside the baseline stability interval. The other two lie beyond it. This is a statement about the baseline, not the new operating point reached after a finite demand step.

Flux exponent control turns such restrictions into a description of possible regulation. Binding determines attainable reaction orders. The catalytic plant and control objective determine which responses are useful. We can then search over regulation subject to the retained constraints without first identifying every binding affinity or regulatory interaction. The next calculation uses a relaxed version of this search to predict transients.

Compare the reaction orders a binding mechanism permits with the reaction orders the cellular task requires. Baseline activity alone cannot make that comparison.

8Optimized enzyme regulation recovers oscillatory ATP transients

Can we recover the qualitative transient without inserting the Hill feedback law? We now ask the structured plant to keep its pools near desired levels while avoiding abrupt activity changes.

Activity control becomes informative only when its freedom is specified. At positive pool concentrations, unconstrained activities can still produce any desired positive fluxes by choosing

u1=vˉ12qˉATP,u2=vˉ22κqˉI.u_1=\frac{\bar v_1}{2\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}},\qquad u_2=\frac{\bar v_2}{2\kappa\bar q_I}.

This would recover the free-flux choice from Section 4. Binding laws, capacity limits or restrictions on how activity can change supply the missing constraints. The next calculation retains the catalytic plant, positive activities and pool floors, and makes activity changes costly. It relaxes the explicit binding reaction-order constraint so that we can examine this dynamic control problem without choosing a molecular mechanism.

Specify a task before selecting a controller. Let qrefq_{\mathrm{ref}} be positive reference pools, QQ the weights on their relative errors, and RR positive weights on changes of log activity. Start from the currently observed pools qcurrentq^{\mathrm{current}} and positive activities ucurrentu^{\mathrm{current}}. Over a future interval of duration TT, consider

min⁡u(⋅)∫tt+T[(log⁡qqref)TQlog⁡qqref+(dlog⁡udt′)TR(dlog⁡udt′)]dt′,subject toq˙=Sv(q,u)+Sww,q(t)=qcurrent,u(t)=ucurrent,q∈X,u∈U.\begin{aligned}\min_{u(\cdot)}\quad&\int_t^{t+T}\left[\left(\log\frac{q}{q_{\mathrm{ref}}}\right)^{\mathsf T}Q\log\frac{q}{q_{\mathrm{ref}}}+\left(\frac{d\log u}{dt'}\right)^{\mathsf T}R\left(\frac{d\log u}{dt'}\right)\right]dt',\\\text{subject to}\quad&\dot q=S v(q,u)+S^w w,\quad q(t)=q^{\mathrm{current}},\quad u(t)=u^{\mathrm{current}},\quad q\in\mathcal X,\quad u\in\mathcal U.\end{aligned}

The sets X\mathcal X and U\mathcal U specify state and actuator restrictions. An ATP floor is one possible state constraint. Activity bounds, allowed regulation channels and mechanism-specific reaction-order restrictions can constrain the controller. Different choices define different performance questions.

The paper solves a sequence of short prediction problems. Model predictive control predicts the future from the current pools, optimizes an activity sequence, applies its first change and replans. The numerical example uses a local linear prediction at each update and advances the nonlinear catalytic plant between updates. The cell need not literally execute this algorithm for the constrained calculation to be informative.6

The experiment asks the controller to reach a new operating condition. As in the published notebook, demand rises from one to 1.1. The target ATP concentration changes from one to 0.93, and the target intermediate concentration changes from 1/κ1/\kappa to 1/κ+0.071/\kappa+0.07. The three optimized responses use increasing costs of activity changes. This is a response to a demand change and a target change together. The comparison with the Hill model concerns the emergence of ringing.

P8Oscillatory transients can emerge from a structured plant and a regulation objective without specifying the Hill mechanism.

A regulation objective can produce ringing without specifying a Hill feedback law. ATP initially falls when demand rises. The activities then change and the pools ring as the controller pursues the specified reference. These are oscillatory transients from the computed controller, not evidence that it has reconstructed the original allosteric mechanism or produced the same sustained oscillation as every Hill-law case.

A molecular implementation is a further construction. To implement the optimized regulation, we would need a binding network and any controller memory that achieve it over the relevant states. The optimized activity trajectory alone does not identify that network.

A steady flux optimum has no corresponding concentration trace. FBA supplies the balanced requirement vˉ1=vˉ2=wˉ\bar v_1=\bar v_2=\bar w. It cannot produce the ATP dip or ringing shown here. Dynamic FBA and other extensions add further assumptions, such as changing external concentrations or biomass. The distinction here is the internal substrate-dependent transient retained by the catalytic plant.

Read an optimized trajectory together with its plant, objective and enforced constraints. Qualitative dynamics can be inferred without identifying every kinetic mechanism.

9An optimizer can pause growth to protect ATP

At steady state, our small pathway left vgrow=v1−wv_{\mathrm{grow}}=v_1-w for growth. That balance assumes production has already adjusted. During a demand increase, the payoff rate depends on the intermediate currently available. Growth now competes with restoring the same ATP pool that must fund the adjustment.

Growth and maintenance draw on the same ATP pool. Keep the three-reaction accounting used in the small flux balance example. The new question is how to allocate ATP while the pools are changing.

dqˉIdtˉ=vˉ1−vˉ2,dqˉATPdtˉ=−vˉ1+2vˉ2−vˉgrow−wˉ.\begin{aligned}\frac{d\bar q_I}{d\bar t}&=\bar v_1-\bar v_2,\\\frac{d\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}}{d\bar t}&=-\bar v_1+2\bar v_2-\bar v_{\mathrm{grow}}-\bar w.\end{aligned}

The bar denotes the same declared concentration, flux and time normalization throughout this calculation. The growth outlet measures allocation of ATP equivalents to growth material. Its time integral is cumulative growth allocation. It is not a specific population growth rate.

To constrain the changing fluxes, retain a dependence on the pools and enzyme activities. The following illustrative rate form follows the reaction structure and fixed partial powers of the growth example in the lecturer's Shenzhen slides. The numerical calculation is new.7

vˉ1=qˉATP−2u1,vˉ2=2qˉIu2,vˉgrow=qˉATPugrow.\bar v_1=\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}^{-2}u_1,\qquad \bar v_2=2\bar q_Iu_2,\qquad \bar v_{\mathrm{grow}}=\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}u_{\mathrm{grow}}.

The first flux already includes an effective inhibitory dependence on ATP. The exponent −2-2 is an assumed reaction order. It is not the number of ATP molecules consumed and is not a bare mass-action law. The first two activities lie between 10−410^{-4} and 11. The growth activity lies between 00 and 11. The rates extend continuously to zero growth activity.

The optimization rewards growth while preserving an ATP reserve. At each observation, predict twenty steps of length Δtˉ=0.1\Delta\bar t=0.1. Let uk=(u1,k,u2,k,ugrow,k)Tu_k=(u_{1,k},u_{2,k},u_{\mathrm{grow},k})^{\mathsf T}, and let u−1u_{-1} be the previously applied activity vector. Choose the activities to minimize

J=∑k=019{0.1[−vˉgrow,k+10(qˉATP,k−1)2]+0.02∥uk−uk−1∥2}.J=\sum_{k=0}^{19}\left\{0.1\left[-\bar v_{\mathrm{grow},k}+10\left(\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP},k}-1\right)^2\right]+0.02\left\|u_k-u_{k-1}\right\|^2\right\}.

The constraints include the nonlinear rate equations, the activity bounds, and the pool floors qˉI≥0.05\bar q_I\geq0.05 and qˉATP≥0.5\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}\geq0.5. The known demand is held constant over each prediction. Only the first chosen activity is applied. The nonlinear dynamics then advance before the next optimization. These are local numerical solutions of a finite-horizon problem, not a proof of a globally optimal cellular strategy.

A maintenance increase can make temporary growth arrest useful for this objective. Raise the demand from 0.60.6 to 1.41.4 at time zero. The pre-step pools are approximately (qˉI,qˉATP)=(0.678,0.859)(\bar q_I,\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}})=(0.678,0.859), with activities (u1,u2,ugrow)=(1,1,0.880)(u_1,u_2,u_{\mathrm{grow}})=(1,1,0.880). The throughput is approximately 1.361.36. The new demand therefore exceeds the existing throughput even if the cell stops allocating ATP to growth. To sustain the higher demand in a new balanced state, the intermediate pool must increase because payoff activity is already at its ceiling.

P9A temporary pause in growth can protect ATP under a stated reserve-and-growth objective.

The pause buys ATP protection by giving up some growth. Over the displayed interval from zero to ten, the policy that permits arrest has the lower executed discrete cost (2.5002.500 versus 2.5542.554). Its cumulative growth allocation is smaller (0.9680.968 versus 1.1071.107). This is a result for the stated growth-and-reserve objective. It does not imply that growth arrest always increases future growth or that every cell uses this objective.

Use the same reaction accounting for a steady allocation bound and a dynamic allocation problem. Then identify which extra kinetic constraints and performance choices make a pause useful.

10Choose constraints that match the cellular function being explained

The biomachine comparison has now supplied a progression of models. Each retains a different amount of the physical machine and therefore answers a different question.

P10A performance bound, a possible transient and an implemented controller are different levels of explanation.

QuestionWhat we retainWhat we compute
Can this chemical network sustain a specified output?Steady stoichiometry, directions, capacities and exchangesFeasible fluxes and a performance bound from FBA
How can regulation manage a disturbance or a transient allocation?Pool dynamics, substrate-dependent catalysis and stated actuator restrictionsOptimized trajectories on a structured metabolic plant
Can the cell implement the proposed regulation?A binding network, enzyme state changes, synthesis and resource constraintsA molecular controller and its operating range

The same ATP-producing machine has answered three different questions. At fixed supply, each unit of steady maintenance demand removes one unit of possible growth allocation. During a disturbance, ATP must pay for production before receiving the payoff. Binding restricts which concentration sensitivities regulation can implement. The growth example then asks how those changing pools alter the allocation decision.

The biomachine perspective connects these answers. Mass balance and feedback principles apply to both cells and engineered chemical plants. The molecular components determine which controls the cell can implement. Optimizing under those restrictions gives a performance bound or a candidate strategy. The claimed function, retained constraints and implemented mechanism remain separate parts of the explanation.

The next missing resource is the machinery itself. We have treated enzyme availability as prescribed or controllable within stated limits. A real cell must make those enzymes from precursors using ribosomes, and every allocation competes with other cellular functions. Lecture 14 closes this loop. It connects metabolic supply to proteome allocation, enzyme production and growth dilution.

Match the prediction to the retained constraints. Then ask what additional machinery and resources would make the proposed behavior physically attainable.

Optional calculations and implementation details

A1 · Where a Hill inhibition factor can come from

A two-state binding approximation produces an integer-exponent Hill factor. Suppose an enzyme has an active unbound state and an inactive state occupied by nn regulatory ligands. Assume binding equilibrium and a regime where intermediate occupancies contribute negligibly to the binding polynomial. Let LL denote the free ligand concentration and KdK_d the effective concentration scale of this binding weight. If the relative equilibrium weight of the occupied state is (L/Kd)n(L/K_d)^n, then

active fraction=11+(L/Kd)n.\text{active fraction}=\frac{1}{1+(L/K_d)^n}.

This is an effective reduction of sequential binding, not an elementary reaction involving the simultaneous arrival of nn ligands. The exponent is an integer in this construction. The noninteger powers used in an effective Hill fit need not count physical binding sites. A general binding network retains intermediate states and need not reduce to this single fraction.

A2 · Derive the stability and sensitivity constraints behind the graphics

The local feedback calculation follows from three rate derivatives. At baseline, ∂vˉ1/∂qˉATP=1−h\partial\bar v_1/\partial\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}=1-h, ∂vˉ2/∂qˉI=κ\partial\bar v_2/\partial\bar q_I=\kappa and ∂vˉ2/∂qˉATP=−g\partial\bar v_2/\partial\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}=-g. Substitution into the two balances gives

Ah=(−κ1−h+g2κh−1−2g),Dh(s)=s2+(κ+1+2g−h)s+κ(h−1).A_h=\begin{pmatrix}-\kappa&1-h+g\\2\kappa&h-1-2g\end{pmatrix},\qquad D_h(s)=s^2+(\kappa+1+2g-h)s+\kappa(h-1).

Negative trace and positive determinant give 1<h<1+κ+2g1<h<1+\kappa+2g. This proves the baseline stability interval in Section 3. A finite demand step changes the operating point and requires a fresh Jacobian. Demand above the maximum investment flux may leave no positive balanced state.

Separate upstream feedback from the plant to identify the relevant control limitation. Let x=δqˉIx=\delta\bar q_I, y=δqˉATPy=\delta\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}, d=δwˉd=\delta\bar w, and let α=δlog⁡u1\alpha=\delta\log u_1 perturb upstream enzyme activity. Retain downstream inhibition gg inside the plant. Before closing upstream feedback, the flux perturbations are δvˉ1=y+α\delta\bar v_1=y+\alpha and δvˉ2=κx−gy\delta\bar v_2=\kappa x-gy. Thus

(x′y′)=(−κ1+g2κ−1−2g)(xy)+(1−1)α+(0−1)d.\begin{pmatrix}x'\\y'\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-\kappa&1+g\\2\kappa&-1-2g\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\alpha+\begin{pmatrix}0\\-1\end{pmatrix}d.

Primes use the normalized clock. Solving the Laplace-transformed matrix equation at zero initial perturbation gives y=Pα+Wdy=P\alpha+Wd, where

D0(s)=s2+(κ+1+2g)s−κ,P(s)=κ−sD0(s),W(s)=−s+κD0(s).D_0(s)=s^2+(\kappa+1+2g)s-\kappa,\qquad P(s)=\frac{\kappa-s}{D_0(s)},\qquad W(s)=-\frac{s+\kappa}{D_0(s)}.

The upstream actuation plant contains both an unstable pole and an inverse-response zero. Its positive pole and positive zero are

p=−(κ+1+2g)+(κ+1+2g)2+4κ2,z=κ.p=\frac{-(\kappa+1+2g)+\sqrt{(\kappa+1+2g)^2+4\kappa}}2,\qquad z=\kappa.

Increasing upstream activity initially spends ATP, even though its later payoff can replenish ATP. This explains the zero's physical origin. Setting g=0g=0 recovers the plant with fixed downstream activity.

Closing the upstream loop gives a dimensionless sensitivity factor. The Hill law has local feedback α=−hy\alpha=-hy. Define the loop transfer Lh=hPL_h=hP. Then

Sh=11+Lh=D0Dh,yd=WSh=−s+κDh(s).\mathcal S_h=\frac1{1+L_h}=\frac{D_0}{D_h},\qquad \frac{y}{d}=W\mathcal S_h=-\frac{s+\kappa}{D_h(s)}.

The calligraphic Sh\mathcal S_h is feedback sensitivity. The plain SS remains the stoichiometric matrix. Since the plant before upstream feedback is unstable, WW is an algebraic reference transfer, not a settled uncontrolled experiment.

The ordinary Bode integral requires its high-frequency hypothesis. For a real-rational, strictly proper, single-input single-output loop with an internally asymptotically stable interconnection and no hidden unstable cancellations, let pjp_j be the right-half-plane poles of the loop transfer. When lim⁡s→∞sL(s)\lim_{s\to\infty}sL(s) is finite,

∫0∞ln⁡∣S(iω)∣ dω=π∑jRe⁡pj−π2lim⁡s→∞sL(s).\int_0^\infty\ln|\mathcal S(i\omega)|\,d\omega=\pi\sum_j\operatorname{Re}p_j-\frac\pi2\lim_{s\to\infty}sL(s).

The loop in Lecture 10's adaptation calculation decays at least as fast as 1/s21/s^2 and has no unstable poles. Its integral is zero. Here lim⁡sLh=−h\lim sL_h=-h, so the ordinary integral is πp+πh/2\pi p+\pi h/2. It changes with gain. This correction is given in Åström and Murray, Exercise 14.3.13

The positive zero supplies a gain-independent weighted identity. Internal stability and a finite controller at zz give Sh(z)=1\mathcal S_h(z)=1. The plant pole gives Sh(p)=0\mathcal S_h(p)=0. Remove that zero by defining F(s)=[(s+p)/(s−p)]Sh(s)F(s)=[(s+p)/(s-p)]\mathcal S_h(s). Its apparent singularity at pp is removable. It has no poles or zeros in the open right half-plane, and ∣F(iω)∣=∣Sh(iω)∣|F(i\omega)|=|\mathcal S_h(i\omega)|. The Poisson integral evaluated at zz therefore gives

2π∫0∞zz2+ω2ln⁡∣Sh(iω)∣ dω=ln⁡∣F(z)∣=ln⁡z+pz−p.\frac2\pi\int_0^\infty\frac{z}{z^2+\omega^2}\ln|\mathcal S_h(i\omega)|\,d\omega=\ln|F(z)|=\ln\frac{z+p}{z-p}.

The factor 2/π2/\pi converts the two-sided integral in Chandra, Buzi and Doyle's supporting material to positive frequencies. The identity applies to the stable gain family plotted in Section 3. With r=(2/π)arctan⁡(ω/z)r=(2/\pi)\arctan(\omega/z), the measure becomes dr=(2/π)z dω/(z2+ω2)dr=(2/\pi)z\,d\omega/(z^2+\omega^2). This is why the last panel's ordinary signed area equals the weighted integral.14

The integral constrains a tradeoff without fixing every transient. It requires amplification somewhere and gives sup⁡ω∣Sh(iω)∣≥(z+p)/(z−p)≈1.971\sup_\omega|\mathcal S_h(i\omega)|\ge(z+p)/(z-p)\approx1.971. It does not set a nonlinear oscillation amplitude or a disturbance threshold. Changing the actuation channels or downstream kinetics changes the control problem. The two controlled activities in Section 8 must be analyzed under their own assumptions.

A3 · From reaction orders to local stability and the general control formulation

Two reaction orders determine baseline stability in the running example. Use the positive balanced state (qˉI∗,qˉATP∗)=(1/κ,1)(\bar q_I^*,\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}^*)=(1/\kappa,1), fluxes vˉ1∗=vˉ2∗=1\bar v_1^*=\bar v_2^*=1, and fixed external demand wˉ=1\bar w=1. Assume upstream flux depends only on ATP and downstream flux is first order in intermediate. The upstream and downstream ATP reaction orders are aa and bb. Therefore

δvˉ1=a δqˉATP,δvˉ2=κ δqˉI+b δqˉATP.\delta\bar v_1=a\,\delta\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}},\qquad\delta\bar v_2=\kappa\,\delta\bar q_I+b\,\delta\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}.

Substituting into the same concentration balances gives the Jacobian in the normalized clock:

A=(−κa−b2κ−a+2b),tr⁡A=−κ−a+2b,det⁡A=−κa.A=\begin{pmatrix}-\kappa&a-b\\2\kappa&-a+2b\end{pmatrix},\qquad\operatorname{tr}A=-\kappa-a+2b,\qquad\det A=-\kappa a.

For κ>0\kappa>0, both eigenvalues have negative real part exactly when the trace is negative and determinant positive. Thus the linearization is asymptotically stable exactly for 2b−κ<a<02b-\kappa<a<0. For b=−0.3b=-0.3 and κ=1.1\kappa=1.1, the interval is (−1.7,0)(-1.7,0). At a=0a=0 one eigenvalue is zero. At a=−1.7a=-1.7 the two eigenvalues are purely imaginary. Nonlinear behavior at either boundary needs a further calculation.

The same slope also controls the steady ATP offset. At a nearby balanced state, vˉ1∗=wˉ\bar v_1^*=\bar w. For a≠0a\ne0, differentiation at the baseline gives

a δqˉATP∗=δwˉ,∂qˉATP∗∂wˉ=1a.a\,\delta\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}^*=\delta\bar w,\qquad\frac{\partial\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}^*}{\partial\bar w}=\frac{1}{a}.

Making the negative slope larger in magnitude reduces the local steady error. The baseline loses stability when the slope crosses the left endpoint. This recovers the Hill result through reaction orders without requiring the full Hill rate law away from the operating point.

Flux exponent control uses these restrictions to describe a family of possible regulations. For positive fluxes v(q,u)v(q,u) and a static regulatory law u=u(q)u=u(q), the chain rule gives

Hvcl←q=Hv←q+Hv←uHu←q,vcl(q)=v(q,u(q)).\boxed{H^{v_{\mathrm{cl}}\leftarrow q}=H^{v\leftarrow q}+H^{v\leftarrow u}H^{u\leftarrow q},\qquad v_{\mathrm{cl}}(q)=v(q,u(q)).}

The entries of Hv←qH^{v\leftarrow q} are ∂log⁡vj/∂log⁡qi\partial\log v_j/\partial\log q_i at fixed activity. The entries of Hv←uH^{v\leftarrow u} describe which activities affect which fluxes. The entries of Hu←qH^{u\leftarrow q} describe the unknown regulatory response. A binding-derived constraint on the left restricts the controllers on the right. The paper denotes these matrices Hcl,HA,HB,HKH^{\mathrm{cl}},H^A,H^B,H^K, respectively.1

The activity factor and its reaction order have different jobs. The positive value uu sets a rate multiplier. Its logarithmic derivative tells us how that multiplier responds when concentrations change. The phrase flux exponent control refers to the regulation of these reaction orders. It does not mean that a numerical activity amplitude is itself an exponent, or that changing enzyme abundance leaves the rate scale unchanged.

Constant partial reaction orders can be integrated into a referenced power law. Choose positive references q∘,u∘q^\circ,u^\circ and v∘=v(q∘,u∘)v^\circ=v(q^\circ,u^\circ). If the two partial-order matrices remain constant over a connected positive domain,

v(q,u)=Λv∘exp⁡ ⁣[Hv←qlog⁡qq∘+Hv←ulog⁡uu∘],q˙=Sv(q,u)+Sww.v(q,u)=\Lambda_{v^\circ}\exp\!\left[H^{v\leftarrow q}\log\frac{q}{q^\circ}+H^{v\leftarrow u}\log\frac{u}{u^\circ}\right],\qquad\dot q=S v(q,u)+S^w w.

Division, logarithms and exponentials act componentwise. Λa\Lambda_a denotes the diagonal matrix with diagonal aa. Reference ratios make the logarithms dimensionless. If the orders vary, freezing them gives a local approximation rather than an exact global rate law.

The closed-loop reaction orders determine the local concentration Jacobian. At a positive balanced operating point, write zq=Λq∗−1δqz_q=\Lambda_{q^*}^{-1}\delta q. For a fixed external disturbance and a static regulatory law,

z˙q=Aqzq,Aq=Λq∗−1SΛv∗Hvcl←q.\dot z_q=A_qz_q,\qquad A_q=\Lambda_{q^*}^{-1}S\Lambda_{v^*}H^{v_{\mathrm{cl}}\leftarrow q}.

Stoichiometry converts flux changes into pool changes. Reaction orders convert relative concentration changes into relative flux changes. The ratios vj∗/qi∗v_j^*/q_i^* set the physical inverse-time scale. Conserved pools require independent coordinates before an inverse state matrix is used.

Binding constraints restrict a controller family. If a specified mechanism has attainable order set P\mathcal P, a static controller must satisfy

Hv←q+Hv←uHu←q∈P.H^{v\leftarrow q}+H^{v\leftarrow u}H^{u\leftarrow q}\in\mathcal P.

A polyhedral outer bound may contain orders that no single biochemical mechanism attains. Pointwise admissible slopes also do not ensure that an arbitrary sequence integrates to a globally realizable rate law. Dynamic regulation needs its own internal states. These are questions beyond merely finding a positive activity trajectory.

A4 · What the published predictive-control calculation solves

The plotted glycolysis computation follows the public notebook's discrete problem. At each update, it freezes the local relative linearization, predicts twenty steps of size 0.03 and optimizes log-activity increments. It applies the first increment and advances the nonlinear plant with constant activity for that interval. The state weight is Q=diag⁡(0.3,0.08)Q=\operatorname{diag}(0.3,0.08). The three increment weights are R=rI2R=rI_2, with r=3,4.25,5.5r=3,4.25,5.5 and I2I_2 the two-dimensional identity matrix.

The notebook's reference schedule is part of the experiment. Demand changes from one to 1.1 at normalized time zero. The desired pools change from (1/1.1,1)(1/1.1,1) to (1/1.1+0.07,0.93)(1/1.1+0.07,0.93). Initial activities are exp⁡(−0.695)\exp(-0.695). The predictor constrains ATP to at least 0.6 and intermediate to at least 0.001. It imposes no activity upper bound or explicit binding-order polytope. The reference values follow the notebook rather than the different values in the printed Figure 5 caption.

The lower bounds remain inactive in these three recomputations. The quadratic problems can therefore be solved using their unconstrained normal equations, with every predicted bound checked afterward. The nonlinear plant is integrated exactly during each interval of constant activity. A different setting that activates a bound needs a constrained solver. A continuous squared-rate penalty and a discrete increment penalty also require different time-step factors, so the stated weights should not be transferred unchanged to another step size.

Teaching route

PartSectionsTimeQuestion answered
Part 1 · A known metabolic machine1–324 minWhat do the components, accounting and kinetics let us predict?
Part 2 · Objectives, constraints and steady prediction4–635 minHow can objectives and constraints specify behavior, and what can a steady relaxation establish?
Part 3 · Structured dynamic prediction7–1036 minWhich biochemical structure restores the transient question?

These blocks total 95 minutes. The optional machine-design extension and supporting calculations are outside the spoken route. If discussion needs more time, show one pair of organism conditions and one growth-arrest comparison. Keep the running glycolysis model and every transition between model levels.
